items.excerpt: Anadolu's recap of top stories from around the globe 13 November 2026• Update: 13 November 2026 BRUSSELS Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Friday, including US President Donald Trump saying he may use military force against Iran "right now" if US allies and ships are threatened, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that a planned prisoner exchange between Russia and Ukraine would be the largest of its kind to date, Israeli strikes killing several in Gaza, and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan calling for stronger global action on climate change at COP31. US President Donald Trump said Thursday that he may use military force against Iran "right now" if US allies and ships are threatened. Asked during an interview with the Salem News Channel whether he would hesitate to use force to stop Iran from "terrorizing our allies and our ships," he answered: "No hesitation. We’re doing very well with it right now." "But the answer is, if I saw things going the other way, I would do that, and it’s possible I would do it right now," he added. Trump claimed the US has suffered no losses in recent months. Asked whether he was willing to maintain the US blockade even if it took 26 months to collapse the Iranian regime, he said: "Well, the regime is collapsing, and their press is much different than the facts." - Ukraine, Russia to hold largest-ever prisoner exchange: Zelenskyy Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a planned prisoner exchange between Russia and Ukraine would be the largest of its kind to date, describing the development as a "real result" of ongoing negotiations. Speaking to reporters after meeting with US President Donald Trump's Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law and Special Envoy Jared Kushner in Dublin, Zelenskyy said the Russian side had agreed on a prisoner exchange. Zelenskyy also said that European representatives would take part in the next round of negotiations as members of the negotiating team, rather than participating separately. The meeting comes after Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Moscow on Thursday for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin. - Israeli attacks kill 11 Palestinians in Gaza Israeli attacks killed 11 Palestinians, including a child, a doctor and a woman, and wounded around 40 others across the Gaza Strip on Thursday, according to medical sources. In the latest attack, a Palestinian man was killed and another moderately wounded when an Israeli drone struck a gathering of civilians in Jabalia al-Nazla in the northern Gaza Strip, a medical source at Al-Shifa Hospital told Anadolu. Earlier, a 35-year-old man and a woman were killed when an Israeli drone struck a civilian vehicle near Al-Shifa Hospital, according to the source. In central Gaza, another man was killed and others were wounded when an Israeli drone struck a civilian vehicle on Al-Baraka Street in Deir al-Balah, said a medical source at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital. On Thursday, an Israeli airstrike hit the second floor of the Al-Yasin building at Nasser Medical Complex in western Khan Younis, killing six and injuring around 30 others, said Gaza’s Civil Defense. - Turkish president says political commitment at COP31 encouraging for efforts under Paris Agreement Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Thursday that the political commitment shown at the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Antalya was a positive sign for advancing the goals of the Paris Agreement, urging sustained determination to keep the 1.5C target within reach. "The political commitment demonstrated in Antalya is encouraging for the work to be carried out under the Paris Agreement. Let us maintain this determination, continue our efforts toward implementation and make the 1.5-degree target achievable," he said in a written statement. Erdogan expressed his "deepest gratitude" to all heads of state and government who attended the summit, stressing that their gathering and direct messages carried particular significance at a time of major international challenge ... - Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid board investigation Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive officer and board member, effective immediately, amid an independent investigation into reports that he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO and will retain her existing responsibilities as the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent successor. His departure follows the board's Nov. 8 announcement of an independent investigation. Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees that day and pledged to cooperate with the inquiry. - Microsoft outage nears 12-hour mark, with no clear timeline for full recovery Microsoft 365 users continued to experience widespread connectivity problems as a major service disruption stretched towards the 12-hour mark, affecting access to Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and other Microsoft services across multiple regions. Despite several recovery measures, Microsoft said its efforts to restore normal service were not progressing as expected, with unexpectedly unavailable servers emerging as the main cause of the disruption. In its latest update on the US social media platform X, Microsoft 365 Status said it had monitored the impact of changes introduced to improve serviceability but confirmed that they were not delivering the expected results.

Health experts blame the outbreaks on falling vaccination rates fueled by disproven claims that the vaccines, which have saved millions of lives globally, are not safe. ... Hunt for clues in deadly Brooklyn building collapse will take time NEW YORK (AP) — New York City’s mayor says two of the eight people killed when an apartment building collapsed in Brooklyn were children. A city official says the three-story building gave way Wednesday afternoon while construction workers were digging at a neighboring lot. The cause is still under investigation. The fire department says the search for victims has ended. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said during a news conference Thursday that two of the victims were construction workers. He says 18 people were injured in the collapse and rescue operation. The mayor has ordered safety inspections at about 100 building sites related to the companies involved in the construction project where the collapse occurred.

items.title: Treasury yields rise as traders strengthen Fed rate hike bets
items.excerpt: Published Fri, Nov 13 2026 3:43 AM EST Updated 4 Min Ago Hugh Leask Treasury yields edged higher on Friday as investor expectations for a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve gathered strength. The 10-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist note yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 2 basis points to 5.1271%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond Add To Watchlist yield, which tends to react to geopolitical risks, was 3 basis points higher at 5.4602%. The 2-year Treasury note Add To Watchlist yield, which is typically more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was 1 basis point lower at 4.8525%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. The upward moves come after 10-year Treasury yields jumped more than 13 basis points to more than 5% during Thursday's session, and the 2-year yield soared more than 15 basis points. Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a near certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a 25 basis points hike now stand at almost 87%, with the chance of a 50 basis point increase at around 13%. Energy inflation remains in focus, with oil set for its second weekly decline as the prospects of renewed strikes by the U.S. against Iran recede. Prices were choppy in early trade Friday. U.S. West Texas Intermediate Add To Watchlist futures for December delivery were down 0.1% at $88.63 per barrel. Brent crude Add To Watchlist was higher by 0.3% at $96.11. October's producer price index — a key measure of wholesale inflation — is due later Friday. It is expected to show 0.4% growth for last month, compared to 1.3% in September's report.

items.title: Hammack Backs Gradual Fed Rate Hikes as October Inflation Gives Mixed Signal | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: By Miriam Hart Nov 13, 2026, 7:15 AM UTC ... Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favors a series of modest rate increases as October U.S. data show slower headline inflation but a steady 0.3% monthly core increase, Reuters reported. At a Nov. 12 discussion with Ohio State University's Fisher College of Business students, Hammack argued that smaller moves made more often would be easier for households and businesses to absorb than larger adjustments. She also supports moving monetary policy into restrictive territory to bring inflation back toward the Fed's 2% goal. The Cleveland Fed's event calendar lists the discussion for 8:30 a.m. ET and provides a recording. Her latest comments extend a position she has outlined before; EconoTimes previously covered Hammack's support for smaller Fed moves. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers rose 0.4% in October, seasonally adjusted, after a 0.6% increase in September. Its index excluding food and energy rose 0.3% in October, matching the monthly increases in August and September. The figures show headline growth slowing while the core measure continued at the same pace. BLS said it could not publish 12-month changes for affected series because it did not collect October 2025 data during a lapse in appropriations. The October release therefore lacks its usual annual comparison for those series. The Fed's longer-run 2% inflation goal is measured using the annual change in the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, a separate measure from CPI. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held the federal funds target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on Oct. 28, in a 10-2 vote. Fed Governor Lisa D. Cook joined Hammack in dissent, preferring a 0.25-percentage-point increase. The next scheduled FOMC meeting is Dec. 8-9.

items.title: US Fed’s John Williams says inflation ‘far too high’ - CNBC TV18
items.excerpt: November 13, 2026 | 07:53 IST ... ## Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams stated that US inflation remains high, requiring further policy action to reach the 2% goal while preserving maximum employment. Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said US inflation remains high and policymakers must take further action to contain price pressures. “Inflation is far too high and it continues to be high even in the latest data,” Williams said Thursday evening at an event in New York. “We’ll need to take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal promptly and on a sustained basis.” At the same time, he said the Fed must be “making sure that we don’t do undue harm to our maximum employment mandate.” Williams also said that overall, the economy doesn’t seem out of balance. After delivering its first interest-rate hike in three years in September, the Fed held rates last month to await clearer economic data. Since then, officials have signalled broad agreement that rates need to rise to address elevated inflation, but they differ on the appropriate pace. Some officials, like Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson, said this week that “further gradual tightening seems appropriate.” But Fed Governor Christoper Waller opened the door to a larger, half-percentage-point hike as early as next month if inflation data for October came in hotter than expected — which it did, shortly after he spoke. Data Clear Williams said that the Fed had agreed in September to assess forthcoming data to get a “clearer picture of what’s going on” and then make a determination on policy at the next meeting. “We’ll continue to do that process,” he said. “I feel that the data is speaking very clearly to us — the economy is strong, labour market continues to strengthen, and inflation is persistent,” he said. “We still have work to do in terms of getting monetary policy to the right place.” Tuesday’s inflation report showed underlying consumer prices, excluding food and energy costs, rose by 0.3% in October from the prior month — topping estimates for a third straight month. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the data “borderline disturbing.” Interest-rate futures now suggest investors expect quarter-point increases at each of the next three meetings, in December, January and March. ... “The US economy not only continues to grow, but actually seems to be strengthening,” the New York Fed chief said. “We’re seeing that also in the labour market. But we’re not seeing signs of the economy overheating, or signs that somehow the economy is out of balance.” Last week, data showed that US job growth surged in October, with the unemployment rate unexpectedly edging down to 4.1%. Overall private-sector payroll growth was the strongest since March.

items.title: House Democratic leaders face fallout over untimely floor vote fumbles
items.excerpt: A week that was supposed to see House Democrats transition seamlessly from a landslide midterm victory to a leadership coronation has instead been pocked by surprise Republican victories on the House floor. Why it matters: Skeptics of Democratic leadership have seized on these strategic fumbles to cast doubt on their much-heralded managerial abilities in the lead-up to the party's leadership elections next week. - "It's really unfortunate that this happened this week when, obviously, that is a narrative we hear leadership portray," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios. - Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said this week has "certainly not given me confidence," and that the election was an "indictment on how our party has been operating thus far, and this is a big part of why." - "We do know that the Democratic caucus has blundered before on things, like whipping the votes to protect NPR last spring," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "We botched that one." What happened: The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to quash an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, with support from all House Democrats present. - The outcome quickly sparked backlash because nearly a dozen House Democrats were absent, many of whom got caught in a traffic jam returning from an Elect Democratic Women event. - That was followed by an incident on Wednesday in which House Republicans passed a veterans bill by voice vote despite Democratic opposition. - The incidents follow a procedural blowup in September in which a pair of centrist House Democrats repeatedly broke with leadership and helped the GOP advance key bills. What they're saying: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), asked about these incidents by Axios, touted a different veterans bill Democrats forced to a successful floor vote on Thursday via a discharge petition. - "House Democrats once again successfully forced a vote on a piece of legislation designed to make life better for the American people," he said. - House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) did not respond to Axios' question and walked off the House floor into her office. The intrigue: Even some current and incoming House Democrats who are voting for Jeffries as speaker acknowledged the vote was a black eye. ... The other side: Other Democrats told Axios the absences were an inevitable reality of Congress, noting that several who missed votes have said they were attending to emergencies. ... There are certain things that are ... Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.). - Others said the upshot is that House Democrats need to do a better job of getting to votes on time: "The general consensus among the new members is on Jan. 3, it's time to lock in," Rep.-elect Matt Little (D-Minn.) told Axios.

items.title: Democrats seek bipartisan path to immigration reform - Newspaper - DAWN.COM
items.excerpt: Anwar Iqbal Published November 13, 2026 Updated November 13, 2026 06:58am • Call for legal status for long-settled immigrants; plan congressional scrutiny of Homeland Security • Democratic states move to curb local agencies’ role in federal immigration efforts WASHINGTON: Democratic lawmakers on Wednesday called for a bipartisan immigration deal, seeking changes to President Donald Trump’s enforcement policies and legal status for long-settled immigrants. The appeal came as Democratic officials in several states and cities moved to limit their agencies’ role in federal immigration operations. Members of the House and Senate, including lawmakers elected last week, held a news conference outside the US Capitol. The group said election results offered an opportunity to revisit an approach deemed politically costly for Republicans. Representative Veronica Escobar, whose Texas district includes the border city of El Paso, said she wanted far-reaching reform but recognised legislation cannot pass without Republican support. “As we continue to have Donald Trump in the White House, and without a supermajority in the Senate, we need Republican support,” she said, adding that comprehensive reform would therefore have to be bipartisan. Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona urged both parties to pursue an agreement before the congressional session ends, or continue negotiations in the next. Republicans long made immigration reform conditional on securing the border. “We have that right now. We did the job,” Gallego said. “Now let’s figure out how to right-size our immigration issue. Let’s figure out how to keep families together.” Representative Sylvia Garcia of Texas proposed starting with the Dream and Promise Act to provide a basis for broader changes when Democrats take control of Congress in January. Concurrently, state and local Democratic administrations moved to limit the role of their police and detention agencies in enforcing federal civil immigration rules. Houston Mayor John Whitmire issued an order barring police from contacting US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) regarding administrative immigration warrants during routine traffic stops and minor, nonviolent violations. Police may still contact ICE when a person booked into jail for a new offence carrying possible jail time also has an administrative warrant. The order removes provisions requiring officers to wait for extended periods for ICE agents to attend traffic stops or detention scenes. Whitmire consulted Texas’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller before acting, describing the move as an att­empt to ease immigrant communities’ anxiety. Whitmire opposed a 2017 Texas law prohibiting sanctuary-city policies when he was a state senator. The move follows major Democratic statewide gains: Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, and James Talarico won a Senate seat. Abbott earlier threatened to withhold over $110 million in safety grants from Houston over its limits on ICE cooperation. Austin and San Antonio are also reviewing their federal arrangements. Similar changes are occurring elsewhere. Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger ordered state law enforcement agencies to end 287(g) agreements with ICE, which authorise participating local officers to carry out specified immigration duties. Maryland Governor Wes Moore signed legislation ending formal 287(g) partnerships between ICE and local agencies. In New York, a law signed by Governor Kathy Hochul requires local detention facilities’ arrangements with federal immigration detention to end by Nov 25 . California continues applying its Values Act, restricting police resources for federal immigration enforcement. In January, Democrats plan to use congressional committee leadership to scrutinise the Department of Homeland Security, investigate enforcement practices and seek records. However, a majority alone cannot undo the president’s policies. Trump can veto legislation, and Senate rules make passing major measures difficult without broader support.

items.title: Celeb roundup: John Legend's SA tour, Kaytranada's return and more entertainment news
items.excerpt: ## 1. John Legend announces three-city South African tour 13-time Grammy Award winner John Legend is scheduled to bring his The Muse Tour to the country in February 2027. The American singer-songwriter will perform in Pretoria on February 20 at SunBet Arena, before heading to the Durban ICC on February 23. His final South African show will take place at Cape Town’s Grand Arena, GrandWest, on February 25. Fans can expect to hear some of his best-known songs, including “All of Me”, “Ordinary People” and “Tonight (Best You Ever Had)”. Mastercard cardholders will have access to a presale beginning on November 11 at 10am, closing on November 13 at 8.59am. Eligible World, World Elite and World Legend cardholders will also have access to selected tickets from November 13 at 9am. ## 2. Yung Miami joins Ndlala Grandeur concert line-up ... American rapper Yung Miami has been added to the international line-up for Ndlala Grandeur Season 1, with her performance scheduled for December 19. The luxury R&B concert series will run across five nights, from December 16 to 20, 2026. Other announced performers include Tamar Braxton, Eric Benét, DVSN, Chante Moore, Jac Ross and actor Ricco Ross, who will host the event. Nicole Murphy is also among the names announced. The extended concert series is set to bring together international R&B performers across the five-day event. ## 3. Kaytranada returns for Milk + Cookies Music Week ... Grammy-winning producer and DJ Kaytranada is returning to South Africa in December, with performances planned for Cape Town on December 18 and Johannesburg on December 20. The shows will launch Milk + Cookies Music Week ahead of the festival’s third edition in January 2027. Rapper Lou Phelps will join him in both cities, alongside local performers. The Cape Town line-up includes Jinji, Kid Fonque, Kudbeu, Mamthug and Tumi Moliko, while MCHLSN, Muzi, Shamiso, Thakzin and Yolophonik are set to perform in Johannesburg.

The same week, the six songs from Eminem's debut album Infinite became available on streaming for the first time.
